stem:
P(A) = 0.3, P(B) = 0.4, and P(A and B) = 0.12.

Are A and B independent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No, because P(A) and P(B) are not equal.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No, because the events both have probabilities less than 1.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes, because A and B cannot both happen.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes, because P(A)P(B) = 0.12 = P(A and B).

rationales.A: Equal probabilities are not required for independence.
rationales.B: Having probabilities less than 1 does not decide independence. Independence is checked by comparing P(A and B) with P(A)P(B): here 0.3 × 0.4 = 0.12, which equals P(A and B), so A and B are independent.
rationales.C: That would describe mutually exclusive events, not independence.
rationales.D: Independence holds when the joint probability equals the product of the marginal probabilities.

stem:
A test reports p = 0.12 and α = 0.05.

Which conclusion is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reject H₀ because p is less than 1.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fail to reject H₀; the result is not statistically significant at the 0.05 level.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The alternative hypothesis is true with probability 0.12.

rationales.A: The p-value is compared with α, not with 1. Here p = 0.12 is greater than α = 0.05, so there is not enough evidence to reject H₀.
rationales.B: We do not prove the null true.
rationales.C: Because p > α, the evidence is not strong enough to reject the null.
rationales.D: That is a common misinterpretation of p-values.

stem:
A principal asks every student in the school to fill out a survey.

What is this called?

rationales.A: A random sample selects only some members of the population by chance. Here every student is asked, so nothing is sampled and the survey is a census.
rationales.B: There is no subsampling by strata here.
rationales.C: A census collects data from every member of the population of interest.
rationales.D: A census may still have nonresponse issues, but it is still a census by definition.

stem:
A two-stage process has P(first success) = 0.3 and P(second success | first success) = 0.5.

What is the probability of success on both stages?

rationales.A: This adds probabilities instead of multiplying along the path.
rationales.C: Multiplies 0.7 (the probability the first stage does not succeed) by 0.5 instead of 0.3 by 0.5: 0.7 × 0.5 = 0.35.
rationales.D: Treats the two probabilities as overlapping events and adds them, 0.3 + 0.5 − 0.15 = 0.65, instead of multiplying 0.3 × 0.5 = 0.15 for both stages succeeding.
